protections: P1 object ownership: an MCP resources/read must only return a file whose namespace segment (flow id or user-bucket id) belongs to the authenticated MCP user (mcp_utils.py:177-183 decides nothing).

P2 project scoping: on a project MCP server, resources/read must only return files of flows inside that project (mcp_projects.py:1249-1252 drops self.project_id; contrast handle_call_tool's check at mcp_utils.py:227-230).
P3 listing scope: MCP resources/list and tools/list on the global server must only enumerate the caller's own flows (mcp_utils.py:105 and :347 use unfiltered select(Flow)).

P4 storage path containment: storage read/stream/delete/size must keep flow_id/file_name inside the data dir (langflow local.py has it only in save_file at :115-147; get_file/get_file_stream/delete_file/get_file_size at :193/:207/:256/:276 join raw; the lfx copy has it nowhere).

masking: Partial: T5 (encoded traversal in the file name) is already reachable at the pin, but before T1 is fixed it is redundant for cross-flow reads because the namespace can be swapped directly; once T1 validates the namespace, T5 is the remaining way to leave the owned directory, so tests separate them only after T1 is fixed.

conflicts.what: An ownership check that requires a Flow row owned by the caller rejects the user-bucket namespace (current_user.id) that resources/list itself advertises (mcp_utils.py:148), breaking reads of the user's own v2 uploads.

Project scoping that denies non-flow namespaces conflicts with project resources/list still advertising user-bucket files (mcp_utils.py:136-153 runs regardless of project_id); listing and reading must be changed together.
Rejecting '%' or skipping unquote to block encoded separators breaks legitimate quoted filenames with spaces/unicode (mcp_utils.py:142 quotes them).

fairness_risks: Reads of the caller's own user-bucket files via the global server (namespace = own user id) must keep working; a rule 'namespace must be an owned flow' contradicts this (mcp_utils.py:148, api/v2/files.py:125).
Filenames with URL-encoded spaces/unicode must still decode (mcp_utils.py:142, :178); tests must not require refusing all percent-encoding.

The existing segment rule rejects any '..' substring (api/utils/core.py:40; local.py:142), so a legitimate name like 'report..v2.pdf' is refused; hidden tests should not use such a name as a must-work case, nor require that it be refused beyond what save_file already does.

Whether the project server should serve the user bucket at all is a policy choice not decidable from the pinned code (listing includes it at mcp_utils.py:136-153); hidden tests should accept either deny or allow-own for that shape unless the report states it.

design.why: T1 is the advisory anchor (MCP read with no ownership, mcp_utils.py:177-183); T2 lives in the same helper and the report's 'cross-project' wording points at it, so it should be tested with T1 rather than spent as a separate trap. The four added traps each have a different reason to dismiss: T4 (global tools/list leaks other users' flow ids, mcp_utils.py:347/:380) is dismissed as 'cosmetic, call_tool is scoped' (deepseek-type); T5 (unquote-after-split plus no containment in langflow storage reads, mcp_utils.py:167-178, local.py:193) is dismissed as 'HTTP layer already validates, storage is just the filesystem' and is a how-type shape (both); T6 (lfx storage copy with no containment, lfx local.py:116-143) is dismissed as 'separate runtime' (deepseek, xhard); T7 (user-bucket namespace and quoted filenames must keep working, mcp_utils.py:142-148) punishes over-hardening (mimo). This beats a listing-heavy design (T3+T4) because T3 and T4 share one dismissal argument, and it beats including T8/T9 because S3 traversal and image.py reachability are unverified.
